name: What office layout changes are hardest to do after construction starts?

mainEntity.name: Which design changes become expensive or disruptive if I change my mind after office construction has already started?
mainEntity.text: Which design changes become expensive or disruptive if I change my mind after office construction has already started?

acceptedAnswer.text: The hardest office layout changes to make after construction starts are the ones that affect multiple trades. Moving walls changes electrical, data, HVAC, sprinkler, and sometimes fire-rated assemblies. Changing plumbing fixture locations can require new rough-ins and inspections. Adding glass fronts, custom millwork, or extra conference rooms can also ripple through the schedule. Even seemingly small changes can force revisions to plans, permit documents, and shop drawings. In Los Angeles projects, late changes are especially expensive because labor, inspections, and material lead times are already locked in. Finish selections are usually easier to swap than the actual layout or systems. If there is any chance the program may change, finalize room count, power needs, and furniture planning before permit release. A little more time in preconstruction almost always costs less than a mid-project redesign.
acceptedAnswer.description: Changes to wall locations, electrical outlets, plumbing fixtures, HVAC zones, glass fronts, and millwork are hardest to make once construction starts. These items affect multiple trades and inspections. Finish swaps are usually easier than structural or systems changes, but late changes can still delay completion.
